# Tools for the paper, from first draft to accepted.

Two Mac apps, a set of pay-per-use manuscript checks, and free tools, all made by one researcher who writes and submits papers too. Prices are listed here, and all on one page. None of it needs an account.

Title: ModernTex - Native LaTeX Editor for Mac | Purplelink LLC

← All products

macOS
Free 7-day trial · $10 to keep · v1.3.0

# ModernTex

A native macOS LaTeX editor for researchers, not a programmer's IDE with LaTeX bolted on. Multi-file editing, synchronized PDF preview, and the full academic manuscript workflow in one app.

Download the free 7-day trial

The trial is the full app for seven days, no account, nothing to enter. Buying is $10 once, with every 1.x update included; the receipt email includes a permanent license key. Already using the trial? Paste that key into the app's "Have a license key?" and the copy you have unlocks straight away; install the paid download once to get updates. Version 1.3.0 · 15 MB disk image · macOS 14 or later · Apple silicon and Intel. Requirements.

In the app

## Source and PDF, always in sync

New in 1.3

## Two things nobody enjoys writing by hand

A TikZ diagram and a results table are both perfectly capable LaTeX, and neither is a pleasant place to start from a blank line and a syntax reference. ModernTex builds both visually and drops in the real source underneath: nothing hidden, nothing you couldn't have typed yourself.

### TikZ Designer

Drag boxes and arrows into place, pick colors from a swatch, resize by the corner, connect two shapes by dragging between them. Start from a flowchart, pipeline, state machine, or tree preset, or a blank canvas. Reopen an existing diagram from the Figures menu to keep editing it instead of redrawing it.

### Table Editor

Paste a range straight from Excel or Google Sheets and it lands in the right cells, growing the table if the data is bigger and leaving the rest untouched if it's smaller. Return moves down a row, ⌥Return breaks a line inside a cell, and dragging a column edge resizes it, the way a spreadsheet does, producing booktabs-style tabular underneath.

Read more about both on the blog →

Features

## Everything the manuscript needs

### Multi-file manuscript navigation

Navigate complex projects with root file detection and a structured sidebar. Jump between chapters, sections, and bibliography files without losing context.

### Three compile modes

Fast, Live, and Full compile modes let you move at the speed you need. Live mode keeps the PDF in sync as you type. Full mode does the deep pass before submission.

### Synchronized PDF preview

Forward and inverse search: click the source to jump to the PDF, click the PDF to jump to the source. Side by side, always in sync.

### Citation management

BibTeX autocomplete that searches your bibliography by author, title, or key, not only the keys you have already cited. Cite-as-you-type with smart suggestions from your .bib files.

### Plain-language error diagnostics

LaTeX error messages are hostile by design. ModernTex translates them into clear explanations with suggested fixes, reducing the debugging spiral that breaks flow.

### Submission readiness checks

Automatically check anonymization, page limits, required sections, and submission packaging before you hit send, so formatting problems are caught before a journal returns the paper.

### Version snapshots

Take a snapshot at any point: before a major revision, after peer review, before resubmission. Diff between snapshots with meaningful context.

### Live TikZ figure editor

Build flowcharts and diagrams by dragging boxes and drawing connections on a canvas. ModernTex generates the TikZ code as you go; insert it at your cursor when it's ready.

### Table editor

Paste a range from Excel or Google Sheets straight into the right cells. Resize columns by dragging, set a table-wide font, and generate clean booktabs-style LaTeX underneath.

### Native macOS experience

Built in Swift for macOS 14+. Native dark and light mode, system fonts, proper keyboard shortcuts, and performance that doesn't make you wait.

Who it's for

## For academic authors

### PhD students

Writing dissertation chapters and conference papers across multiple files, with deadlines and a committee watching over your shoulder.

### Faculty & researchers

Managing journal submissions, coauthor workflows, multiple concurrent manuscripts, and the full resubmission lifecycle.

### Technical coauthors

Jumping into someone else's LaTeX project and needing to understand the structure, fix compilation issues, and contribute without breaking things.

Not the right fit if several co-authors need to type in the same document at the same moment (keep Overleaf for that draft), you work on Windows, Linux or an iPad, or you would rather not have a TeX distribution on your Mac. ModernTex is also new, first released in September 2026, so it has less of a track record than TeXShop or Texifier. The comparison of Mac LaTeX editors covers the alternatives.

At a glance

Before you install

## What ModernTex needs.

A Mac running macOS 14 or later and a TeX distribution. MacTeX or TinyTeX both work, and you do not have to set either up first: if ModernTex cannot find one when you compile, it offers a one-click TinyTeX install right in the editor. After checkout you get a signed disk image: open it and drag ModernTex to Applications. Bookmark the download page; it always hands you the newest version.

Want one email when a notable version ships? Leave your address. No newsletters, no follow-ups.

Your email is used for release notes and nothing else. Privacy Policy · Why ModernTex →

## Frequently asked questions

How do I get updates?

ModernTex checks for a new version once a day and offers to install it in place. You can also choose Check for Updates from the ModernTex menu at any time. Updates are included in the purchase, and each download is code-signed by Purplelink LLC.

What macOS version is required?

ModernTex requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later.

I lost my license key. How do I get it back?

Enter the email address you used at checkout on the Find a purchase page. If that address bought ModernTex, a new license key and your download page are emailed to that address. Any key you had before keeps working.

Is there a free trial?

Yes. The trial is the complete app for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account and nothing to enter. When it ends, the window shows a notice and a Buy button; your .tex files are ordinary files on disk and are not touched. When you buy, the receipt email includes a license key: paste it into the trial's "Have a license key?" and that same copy unlocks, with no reinstall. The trial copy does not update itself, so install the paid download from your receipt page once to get updates in place.

What does it cost?

$10, once, after a free 7-day trial. That covers every 1.x update. There is no subscription and no account; the optional AI features run on Apple Intelligence or your own Claude or OpenAI account.

How is ModernTex different from TeXShop or Overleaf?

ModernTex is a native macOS app designed specifically for the academic manuscript workflow. It is not a web app and not a general-purpose code editor. It combines multi-file manuscript navigation, synchronized PDF preview, BibTeX autocomplete that searches by author or title, plain-language error diagnostics, and submission-readiness checks. Designed for researchers, not programmers.

Coming from Overleaf: download the project as a zip, or clone it with Overleaf's Git integration, and open the folder. The files stay ordinary .tex, .bib and image files, so you can upload them back to Overleaf or open them in TeXShop at any time. There is no real-time co-editing; for a draft several people type in at once, keep Overleaf. See how the best LaTeX editors for Mac compare, or read what changes when you move from Overleaf to a Mac editor.

Why not just use a free editor like TeXstudio?

TeXstudio is free, cross-platform, and already parses compile errors into a readable list, so it's a legitimate choice, especially if you also work on Windows or Linux. ModernTex is narrower on purpose: Mac only, built around the manuscript workflow specifically. Three things TeXstudio doesn't do: BibTeX autocomplete that searches your whole .bib by author or title rather than just the keys already cited in the file, submission-readiness checks for what journals actually reject on, and an anonymized export for double-blind review. If none of those matter to you, TeXstudio is a perfectly good free option.

Does ModernTex support multi-file projects?

Yes. ModernTex has built-in multi-file manuscript navigation with root file detection and a structured sidebar for jumping between chapters, sections, and bibliography files without losing context.

## Try it on your own manuscript.

Seven days of the full app, no account and nothing to enter. If it earns a place in your workflow, it's $10 once, with every 1.x update included.

# Vitae

Academic research management for macOS. Track submissions, grants, projects, collaborators, and your CV in one local-first app. Free, notarized, no App Store.

Download for Mac
Vitae Plus, 7 days free

Requires macOS 15 Sequoia or later · Apple-notarized · Your data stays on your Mac

What's inside

## Everything an academic needs, nothing they don't

### Submission tracking

Log every journal and conference submission with status, dates, each review round, and the decision. Pick target venues with published acceptance rates for about 13,700 journals and conferences, and get a forecast of publication timelines from your own submission history.

### Grant management

Track NSF, NIH, and other grants from planning to award: deadlines, requested and awarded amounts, reporting dates, and your share. Search Grants.gov for open funding opportunities from inside the app.

### CV & packages

Start from the CV you have. Vitae imports it from Word, PDF, RTF, ODT, or a web page, in APA, Chicago, MLA, IEEE, ACM, Harvard, or Vancouver style, reads your papers, grants, positions, talks, teaching and service, and shows you everything before saving. From then on your CV fills itself from your records. Choose from seven CV formats or build your own, and export several at once to PDF, LaTeX, or rich text that opens in Word. Word (.docx) templates are part of Vitae Plus.

### Inbox triage

Connect iCloud, Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, Fastmail, or your university mail, read-only. Vitae recognizes messages from journal submission systems, reads them on your Mac, and proposes submission updates. You review each one before anything changes.

### Collaborators & projects

Track coauthors, collaborators, and projects. Link people to papers, grants, and roles so your network stays navigable. Send any publication to Zotero in one click.

### Local-first & private

Everything is stored on your Mac with SwiftData. No account and no cloud sync required, and keeping your record needs no subscription. Vitae takes a daily backup and lets you undo changes, so a bad import or merge is never permanent.

Free & open to support

## Vitae is free. If it saves you time, consider supporting it.

All core record-keeping is free, with no limits, and nothing that was free before Plus becomes paid. No third-party ads, no data harvesting. Vitae Plus is an optional subscription, $3 a month or $24 a year, for newer tools such as reports, Word templates, the revision workspace and Shareables. Subscribing, or leaving a one-time tip, helps keep Vitae maintained and updated.

Vitae Plus, from $3 a month
Leave a one-time tip

## Frequently asked questions

Is Vitae really free?

Yes. Vitae is free to download and use, with all core record-keeping and no limits, and nothing that was free before Plus becomes paid. An optional subscription, Vitae Plus ($3 a month or $24 a year, with a 7-day free trial), adds newer tools: reports such as an NIH biosketch draft, Word export with your own templates, the revision workspace, Shareables, the collaboration map, batch DOI lookup and ORCID sync, Reminders and calendar sync, and themes. You do not need it to keep your record. A tip via Buy Me a Coffee is also appreciated but never required.

Does Vitae show ads?

Not from anyone else. The sidebar has one small card, labelled "From Purplelink", that suggests another Purplelink tool such as ModernTex, Paper Review or Vitae Plus. If a sponsor ever appears there, the card will say "Sponsor" and the sponsor's name, and this page will say so. There is no ad network, no tracking, and no click reporting, and Vitae sends nothing to sponsors. Vitae reads the card's text from a plain file on purplelink.llc at most once a day, and shows a copy built into the app when you are offline. You can hide the card in Settings, under Support; Vitae then stops fetching it.

How does Vitae update?

From version 0.3, Vitae checks purplelink.llc once a day and asks before installing a new version. Updates are signed, and Vitae refuses any that fail the check. You can turn the daily check off, or check by hand, in Settings under About. Version 0.1 cannot update itself; download the current version once from this page and it will keep itself up to date after that.

Why isn't it on the Mac App Store?

Distributing outside the App Store lets me ship faster and avoid App Store restrictions. The DMG is Apple-notarized, so macOS Gatekeeper verifies it is safe to run. Just open the DMG, drag Vitae to Applications, and launch it.

What macOS version is required?

Vitae requires macOS 15 Sequoia or later.

Where is my data stored?

All your records are stored locally on your Mac using SwiftData, with no account and no sync. Vitae goes online for lookups you ask for, such as citation counts from Crossref or OpenAlex and Grants.gov funding searches, and reads your email only if you connect a mailbox, read-only. It also makes two small requests to purplelink.llc on its own: the daily update check, and the daily fetch of the sidebar card's text unless you hide the card. Neither sends anything about you or your records. iCloud sync is supported in the schema and can be enabled in future versions.

How do I install it?

Download the DMG, open it, drag Vitae into your Applications folder, and launch it. Because it is notarized by Apple, you will not see a Gatekeeper warning.

How does Vitae compare to Interfolio, ORCID, or a spreadsheet?

Vitae keeps your own record between deadlines; if your university requires Interfolio or Watermark for tenure review, you still submit there, using what Vitae exports. See how to track your academic CV and tenure case for a comparison of sixteen options.

Vitae is free. If it saves you time, you can get the optional Vitae Plus, leave a tip or support it monthly. It helps keep it maintained.

What Plus adds

Deadlines synced to Reminders, and a calendar file that stays up to date.

What stays free

## Your record, with no limits

Submissions and review rounds, grants, projects, collaborators, teaching, service and mentoring, the tenure view, inbox triage, citation counts, CV and package exports to PDF, rich text and Markdown, backups, and updates are all free, with no limits on how much you keep.

Everything Vitae did before Plus, and all core record-keeping, stays free forever. Plus does not unlock any of it, and not subscribing takes nothing away.

How it works

## A key, a monthly check, and cancel anytime

### Paste the key once

When checkout finishes, this site shows a key. In Vitae, open Settings, then Vitae Plus, paste it and press Activate. There is no account and no sign-in.

### Checked by a short key

Your subscription is checked by a short key the app refreshes about once a month; the refresh sends only an anonymous key ID. Between refreshes, Vitae verifies the key on your Mac.

### Cancel anytime

In Vitae, open Settings, then Vitae Plus, then Manage Subscription. Plus keeps working through the period you have paid for, then the Plus tools stop. More on cancelling.

## Frequently asked questions

Do I need Vitae Plus to use Vitae?

No. Vitae is free, with all core record-keeping and no limits. Nothing that was free before Plus becomes paid. Plus adds newer tools built on top of your record.

What happens if I cancel?

Plus keeps working through the period you have paid for, then the Plus tools stop. Your records and every free feature are untouched, and files you already exported are yours.

Does Vitae contact a server to check the subscription?

About once a month, while Plus is active. The app sends only the key's anonymous ID; our server looks up the subscription's status in Stripe and returns a fresh key. Nothing about your records is sent. See the privacy policy.

How do I cancel?

In Vitae, open Settings, then Vitae Plus, then Manage Subscription. We email a link to the address you used at checkout; it opens Stripe's billing page, where you can cancel or update your card. You can also email ben@purplelink.llc. See managing your subscription.

What if I lose my key?

Enter the email address you used at checkout on the key recovery page, and a current key is emailed to that address. The email you got when you subscribed also links to a page that shows a current key.

## Sample report

What does the report look like? Show or hide

An excerpt from an example report on a machine-learning paper. Every finding quotes the passage it is about.

### Critical blind spots

- 
Hyperparameter search asymmetry favors the proposed method.
Quoted: "We tuned learning rate and batch size on the validation set; baselines used reported defaults."
Surfaced by: Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic (consensus).
Fix: Match the search budget for each baseline and report the protocol in the methods section.

### Data-to-claim contradictions

- Claim: "Our method beats all baselines by a wide margin."
Evidence: Table 2 shows the proposed method tied with Baseline C within reported standard errors on 4 of 7 datasets.

### Rectification checklist

- A Add the hyperparameter search protocol to the methods (page 5, Section 3.2).

- B Reference [17] only weakly matches its CrossRef entry; check the title and DOI.

- C Figure 3's y-axis breaks 0-60 then jumps to 90; redraw on a continuous scale.

### References and citation support

47 of 52 references verified against CrossRef; 3 weak title matches to re-check.

Claim "Method X reduces error by 40%" cites [14], whose abstract reports a 4% reduction. Verdict: contradicted.

Read the full example report, with a note on each section →

## How the review works

- 
Layer 1: figure-integrity scan.
Every page is rendered and reviewed for digital manipulation
concerns, figure-vs-text contradictions, and presentation issues
(broken y-axes, missing error bars, color-only encoding).
Hedged language; flags concerns to investigate, never accusations.

- 
Layer 2: citation support audit.
Every reference is verified against CrossRef, then we go deeper:
for the most load-bearing claims, we fetch the cited source's
abstract and check whether it actually supports the claim you
attached it to. Each finding shows your claim next to the source's
own words, with a verdict: supported, partially supported, not
supported by the abstract, contradicted, or source unavailable.
Hedged language; verify each against the full text.

- 
Layer 3: a four-reviewer panel.
Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic, Data Integrity Officer,
and Editor-in-Chief each red-team the paper in parallel.
Findings are merged with a cross-persona consensus filter so
issues raised independently by multiple personas surface first.

- 
Layer 4: the report.
A final pass produces the structured report you'll act on:
critical blind spots, data-to-claim contradictions, an A/B/C
rectification checklist, and an honest novelty estimate.

## What you get

- One review of one manuscript (up to 20 MB PDF, ~100 pages). To have supplementary material read too, merge it into the same PDF.

- An anonymity scan for double-blind submission on every tier: author names, institutions, funders, protocol numbers and self-citations left in the text.

- A Markdown report and an annotated PDF with comments on the pages they refer to.

- Standard reviews are usually ready in 4-8 minutes, Deep Review in 10-15, on a status page that updates itself.

## Frequently asked questions

What does the review include?

Four layers in sequence: a Claude Vision pass over your figures and tables, a live CrossRef cross-check of every reference, an adversarial four-persona reviewer debate (Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic, Data Integrity Officer, Editor-in-Chief) with consensus filtering, and a synthesis pass producing critical blind spots, data-to-claim contradictions, a prioritised rectification checklist, and a true-novelty estimate.

How long does it take?

Typically 4-8 minutes for a 20-page manuscript. You don't need to keep the tab in the foreground. The status page polls until the review is ready and renders it inline.

What about my privacy? Is the manuscript stored?

Your manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API for analysis. Anthropic retains inputs for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, and does not use them for model training. Purplelink itself does not store your manuscript or the resulting review after delivery: the review is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do on the status page. Save the result locally before closing the tab.

Which journals does the Journal Pack check?

25 venues. The pack checks word and abstract limits, required sections and reference-style hints against the one you pick at upload.

- Machine learning: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, TMLR, JMLR

- General science: Nature, Science, Cell, PLOS ONE

- Medicine: Nature Medicine, JAMA, NEJM, The Lancet, The BMJ

- Psychology and management: Psychological Science, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Cognition, Academy of Management Journal

- Chemistry and materials: JACS, Angewandte Chemie, Nature Materials, Nature Chemistry, ACS Nano, Advanced Materials

Not listed? The Standard tier covers everything except this check. Email to ask for a venue.

Is there a referral credit?

Yes. Every report ends with a link carrying your own code. When a colleague opens it and buys a review with a .edu email address, you each receive a single-use $2 code by email. The link counts for 30 days in the browser that opened it.

What domains does it cover?

You pick one of five domain profiles at upload: Machine Learning, Biomedicine, Psychology and Social Science, Chemistry and Materials, or General. Each profile tells the reviewers which failure modes matter most in that field; each link lists them.

How deep is the citation check?

Two levels. First, every reference is checked for existence against CrossRef (dead DOIs, hallucinated or weakly-matched titles). Second, for the most load-bearing claims we fetch the cited source's abstract from OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, or CrossRef and assess whether it supports your claim. This is an abstract-level check: a claim supported only in the full text is marked "not supported by abstract," not wrong. Verify it against the source. When no abstract can be retrieved, the citation is marked "source unavailable" rather than guessed. On citation-heavy papers we audit the most important claims first and tell you how many were not audited.

Am I allowed to use an AI review on my own manuscript?

Yes, under the policies of the major publishers and venues we have checked. Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, IEEE, ACM, ICMJE and NeurIPS let authors use AI tools while preparing a manuscript; the rule against uploading manuscripts to AI is for reviewers, who hold someone else's work. Paper Review writes nothing into your paper, so most disclosure rules, which cover AI-generated text, do not obviously apply; if your venue's policy is strict, a one-line note is enough. The policy guide compares ten publishers and venues.

Is this a replacement for peer review?

No. Treat it as a first-pass red team before you submit: a way to catch the obvious problems a real reviewer will flag before they do. The review is advisory only; you remain responsible for every decision about your manuscript.

What if the review misses something or makes a mistake?

AI reviewers can be wrong. The output flags concerns with hedged language and quotes the manuscript when challenging a claim, so you can verify every finding against your text. If a specific result reads as low-quality, email ben@purplelink.llc and we'll refund the price.

What file format?

PDF up to 20 MB. If you're submitting LaTeX, compile to PDF first (our free LaTeX-to-PDF tool works).

What about clinical or patient data?

Do not submit unredacted patient data. The manuscript will be sent to Anthropic's API with 30-day retention. For papers containing identifiable health information, redact before upload.

Title: Example Paper Review Report: What an AI Pre-Submission Review Finds | Purplelink

← Paper Review

Example report

# What a Paper Review report looks like

This is an example report for a fictional machine-learning manuscript, shown the way you would read it, with a note after each section on what it is for and how to act on it. A real report quotes your own text, and also comes as a Markdown file and an annotated PDF with each comment on the page it refers to.

## Critical Blind Spots

- 

Hyperparameter search asymmetry favors the proposed method.
Quoted: "We tuned learning rate and batch size on the validation
set; baselines used reported defaults."
Surfaced by: Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic (consensus).
Fix: Match search budget for each baseline; report the protocol
in the methods section.

- 

Sample-size justification missing for the human evaluation (Experiment 2).
Quoted: "We recruited 24 annotators ... yielding sufficient
statistical power."
Surfaced by: Statistical Skeptic.
Fix: Replace the claim with a sensitivity analysis: the smallest effect 24 annotators can detect at 80% power. Report confidence intervals for the preference rates, not p-values alone.

What this section is for. The problems a reviewer is most likely to raise. Each one quotes the passage it is about, names which of the four reviewers raised it, and says what would fix it. Findings raised by more than one reviewer are marked as consensus and listed first.

## Data-to-Claim Contradictions

- Claim: "Our method beats all baselines by a wide margin."
Evidence: Table 2 shows the proposed method tied with Baseline C
within reported standard errors on 4 of 7 datasets.

What this section is for. Places where the text claims more than the tables and figures show. Reviewers catch these quickly, and they are usually a wording fix rather than new work.

## Rectification Checklist

- A Add hyperparameter search protocol to methods (page 5,
Section 3.2). Match search budget across all baselines.

- A Replace "wide margin" framing in abstract and Section 5
with what the data actually shows.

- B Add per-seed variance to all results tables.

- B Reference [17] only weakly matches its CrossRef entry;
check the title and DOI.

- C Figure 3's y-axis breaks 0-60 then jumps to 90; redraw on
a continuous scale.

What this section is for. The same findings as a to-do list. A items are the ones a reviewer would reject over; B items weaken the paper; C items are polish. Work through the A items first.

## True Novelty Estimate

The core architectural contribution is genuinely novel and not
covered by [11] or [23]. The empirical comparison, as currently
framed, oversells the gap. Marginal advance: the proposed mechanism
is interesting but the published evidence does not yet warrant the
strength of the abstract's claim.

What this section is for. A plain read of what is new in the paper and whether the evidence supports how strongly it is claimed. Useful for the abstract and the cover letter.

## Reference Verification Summary

47 of 52 references verified against CrossRef. 3 had weak title
matches (re-check [12], [17], [31]). 2 had no DOI and could not be
located by title, verify these are correctly cited.

What this section is for. Every reference is looked up in CrossRef. Weak matches and unresolvable entries are listed so you can check them, which catches typos and citations an AI tool invented.

## Citation Support Audit

Verdicts: 18 supported, 4 partially supported, 2 not supported by
abstract, 1 contradicted, 3 source unavailable.

Claim
Cited ref
Verdict
What the source's abstract says

"Method X reduces error by 40%."
[14]
Contradicted
Abstract reports a 4% reduction, not 40%. Verify the figure.

"Prior work proved this is optimal."
[9]
Not supported by abstract
Abstract describes a heuristic; optimality may be in the full text.

5 citations with weaker claims were not audited (per-run cap).

What this section is for. For the claims that lean hardest on a citation, the cited paper's abstract is fetched and compared with what you wrote. "Not supported by abstract" means check the full text, not that the citation is wrong.

Standard review $9, with the Journal Pack $11, Deep Review $15. A Standard review is usually ready in 4 to 8 minutes. No account, and the file is deleted soon after you open the report. If a report reads as low quality, email within 14 days for a refund.

Per-Comment Tracker

#
Reviewer comment
Verdict

R1.2

Addressed. Power analysis added to Section 3.2.

R1.4

# Citation Gap Analysis

The reverse of a citation-verifier: find prior art the manuscript should cite but doesn't. Catches the "you ignored my paper" reviewer complaint before it happens.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

### Citation Gap Analysis

Result: 5 potential gaps flagged.
Each entry below is a citation a domain reviewer might expect to see. Verify each suggestion against your own knowledge before adding — AI recall can be wrong.

Meta-analytic evidence on sleep deprivation and cognition

- Type: Missing Canonical Paper

- Suggested authors: J. Lim, D. F. Dinges

- Title hint: A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1037/a0018883

- What should be cited: The standard meta-analysis of how short-term sleep loss affects attention, working memory, and other cognitive domains.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The introduction claims sleep loss "impairs complex reasoning" using only two small studies. A sleep researcher would expect the meta-analysis behind that claim.

- Section to add it: Introduction

Dose-response effects of partial sleep restriction

- Type: Missing Prior Finding

- Suggested authors: H. P. A. Van Dongen, G. Maislin, J. M. Mullington, D. F. Dinges

- Title hint: The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects on neurobehavioral functions and sleep physiology from chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1093/sleep/26.2.117

- What should be cited: The controlled study showing that deficits from repeated nights of restricted sleep accumulate over time.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The limitations paragraph says chronic restriction "may differ" from one night but does not cite the work that measured exactly that difference.

- Section to add it: Discussion, limitations

Psychomotor Vigilance Task as the manipulation check

- Type: Missing Framework

- Suggested authors: D. F. Dinges, J. W. Powell

- Title hint: Microcomputer analyses of performance on a portable, simple visual RT task during sustained operations

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.3758/BF03200977

- What should be cited: The original description of the reaction-time task the manuscript uses to confirm participants were sleep restricted.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The PVT is used in Section 3.3 without a source for the task or its lapse threshold.

- Section to add it: Methods, Section 3.3

Origins of defect detection in code inspection

- Type: Missing Canonical Paper

- Suggested authors: M. E. Fagan

- Title hint: Design and code inspections to reduce errors in program development

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1147/sj.153.0182

- What should be cited: The foundational paper on structured code inspection, which introduced defect detection rate as a measure of review effectiveness.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The dependent variable is defect detection rate, and the related work section starts with modern pull-request review without acknowledging where the measure comes from.

- Section to add it: Related work

Prior experiments on sleep loss and developer performance

- Type: Qualitative Gap

- Suggested authors: (unknown)

- Title hint: unknown

- Verification: No searchable title — AI recall only, unverified

- What should be cited: Earlier controlled experiments that measured programming or software-engineering task performance after a night of sleep deprivation.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The manuscript describes itself as the first study of sleep and developer performance. A reviewer familiar with this small literature may question that claim.

- Section to add it: Related work; also soften "first" in the abstract

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What it flags

- Canonical papers in the field that any expert reviewer would expect cited.

- Method or framework foundational references the manuscript builds on without citation.

- Near-identical prior findings the authors should differentiate against.

- Dataset, technique, or theory references missing from the bibliography.

Each suggestion is tagged with the section it belongs in, why a reviewer would notice the omission, and (when known) the candidate authors and title. Always verify suggestions against your own field knowledge. AI recall can be wrong.

## FAQ

How does this differ from the bibliography validator?

The free BibTeX Validator checks the citations you DO have for accuracy and existence. This tool finds the citations you DON'T have but should. Different direction.

What if it suggests papers that aren't actually relevant?

AI recall is imperfect. We mark each suggestion as a candidate to verify, not a definitive call. If a specific scan is low-quality, email ben@purplelink.llc and we'll refund the $3.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The scan result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Anonymity Check

Before you hit submit on a double-blind manuscript, run a leak scan. Flags author names, institution mentions, grant numbers, IRB protocols, self-citation patterns, named software artifacts, and author-owned URLs, anywhere they slipped into the body.

- Pay through Stripe

- Upload the manuscript PDF; the link is also emailed, so you can upload from another device

- Read the result on the page, or ask to be emailed when it is ready

Secure checkout via Stripe. One-time payment.

Deleted soon after delivery. The result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do, and if it reads as low-quality we'll refund the $2.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

### Anonymity Check

Result: 6 potential leaks detected.
Each item below should be removed or generalised before double-blind submission.

Self-citation patterns

- [CRITICAL] Section 2, related work: "In our previous work [14], we found that review accuracy declines after the first hour of a session."

- Fix: Rewrite in the third person ("Prior work [14] found ...") and keep [14] as an ordinary reference.

Institutions

- [MAJOR] methods section: "Participants were recruited from the professional master's program at [University Name]."

- Fix: Replace the name with "a large public university".

IRB and ethics protocol numbers

- [MAJOR] methods section, ethics statement: "The study was approved by the [University Name] IRB under protocol 2024-0917."

- Fix: Write "approved by the authors' institutional review board" and withhold the protocol number until acceptance.

Funding and grants

- [MAJOR] page 14 acknowledgements: "This work was supported by NSF grant #[Grant Number]."

- Fix: Remove the acknowledgements from the review copy and restore them in the camera-ready version.

Emails and URLs

- [CRITICAL] page 6 footnote 3: "Materials and analysis scripts are available at github.com/[username]/sleep-review-study."

- Fix: Link an anonymized copy of the repository for review, with commit history and author names removed.

Named software, datasets and systems

- [MINOR] Section 3.2: "Defects were seeded with ReviewSeed, the tool we released last year."

- Fix: Call it "a defect-seeding tool" and cite it as an anonymized reference.

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What it catches

- Author or co-author names in the body (e.g. "Smith et al." referring to the authors' own prior work).

- Institution names: "at our institution X", lab names, hospital names.

- Funder names and grant numbers ("NSF #1234567", "NIH R01…").

- IRB / IACUC / ethics-board protocol numbers tied to a specific institution.

- Author email addresses, author-owned GitHub repos, lab webpages.

- Named software or datasets that trivially identify the authors.

- "In our previous work [12]" self-citation patterns.

## FAQ

What about acknowledgements?

We scan the body and abstract. Acknowledgement sections often live at the end of the manuscript and we'll catch leaks there too, but always review them manually before submission, especially if your editor strips them automatically.

Is this a replacement for manual blinding?

No. It's a safety net. Manual review of figures, supplementary materials, and metadata is still required.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The scan result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Cover Letter Generator

A draft journal cover letter, calibrated to the journal you're submitting to. No hype, no superlatives. Built from your abstract and the journal name. We never receive your full manuscript.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

Dear Editor,

Please consider our manuscript, "One Night Short: Sleep Restriction and Defect Detection in Code Review," for publication in Empirical Software Engineering.

Our central finding is that a single night of restricted sleep was associated with a measurable drop in how many seeded defects experienced developers caught during code review.

We believe the work fits the journal's focus on empirical studies of software engineering practice. Code review is a routine quality gate in most teams, yet the conditions under which reviewers work are rarely measured. The manuscript may interest readers working on reviewer performance, human factors, and the design of review workflows.

In a within-subjects experiment, 42 professional developers reviewed matched pull requests once after a normal night of sleep and once after a night restricted to four hours, in counterbalanced order. Each change contained seeded defects of known type. Mean detection fell from 61% to 48% under restriction, with the largest drop for logic errors, while the number of false-positive comments did not change. The sample came from a single organization, and the effect may differ for chronic sleep loss; we discuss both limitations.

This manuscript has not been published previously and is not under review elsewhere.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

[Corresponding Author Name]
[Signature]

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What you get

- 200-350 word draft cover letter, calibrated to the journal's scope.

- Methodology and key result summarised in plain prose.

- Originality affirmation included.

- Reviewer suggestions only when the abstract makes the expertise obvious, never invented.

- Plain prose with paragraph breaks; placeholder for your contact name and signature.

## FAQ

Why no PDF upload?

Cover letters are 95% built from the abstract and the target journal's scope. Skipping the full manuscript means we send much less of your unpublished IP to a third-party AI service. The trade-off: the letter cites the manuscript only at the level of detail your abstract supports.

Can you target a specific reviewer or editor?

You can paste an "author note" with that context when you compose. The model will weave it into the letter if it fits naturally.

What model produces the letter?

Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5 with temperature 0.1. The same model + settings that power our main Paper Review tool.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The letter is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. Your abstract and journal name are sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Resume Review

Would this resume clear an ATS filter and make a hiring manager read past the first six seconds? A three-persona AI panel (ATS Screener, Hiring Manager Skeptic, Recruiter Red Flags) reads your resume the way the people actually screening it would.

## Sample report

What does the report look like? View sample

### Resume Review

ATS Compatibility

- Section header "Experience" is fine, but "Where I've Worked" (used for
the second job block) won't parse: most ATS filters look for a small
set of standard headers. Rename to "Experience" or "Work History."

- Dates in "Jan 2022 - Present" format parse correctly. The single entry
written as "22-24" does not; spell out the years.

Content & Impact

- "Responsible for managing social media accounts" is a duty, not a
result. Rewrite using a number you already have on this resume:
"Grew Instagram following from 4,200 to 11,800 followers in 9 months."

- Three bullets in the 2021 role start with "Helped with...": pick the
one concrete outcome each bullet is actually describing and lead with
that instead.

What a Recruiter Would Flag

- 7-month gap between the Acme and Globex roles isn't explained anywhere
on the resume. Doesn't need a paragraph, just a single line ("Family
leave, 2022") to keep a recruiter from guessing.

- Job title says "Senior Analyst" here but "Analyst II" on LinkedIn per
your notes; pick one and make them match.

Action Checklist

- [A] Rename "Where I've Worked" to "Experience."

- [A] Add the missing number to the social-media bullet.

- [B] Add a one-line explanation for the 7-month gap.

- [C] Reconcile the job title between this resume and LinkedIn.

## What the report includes

- ATS Compatibility. Formatting, section headers, and date-format issues that would break an Applicant Tracking System's parsing, before a human ever sees the resume.

- Content & Impact. Every bullet that reads as generic duty-listing instead of a quantified result, with a suggested rewrite using only the facts you already gave it.

- What a Recruiter Would Flag. Employment gaps, short stints, inconsistent dates, missing basics, framed as what would come up in a first-pass screen, not a judgment.

- Action Checklist. A/B/C-prioritised list of what to fix before you send this resume out.

## FAQ

What file formats do you accept?

PDF or DOCX, up to 20 MB.

Will this rewrite my resume for me?

No. It critiques what you have and suggests specific rewrites for weak bullets, but you decide what to change. It won't invent facts, dates, or metrics you didn't provide.

Does it check for ATS compatibility?

Yes. One of the three personas specifically simulates how an Applicant Tracking System would parse your resume's formatting, section headers, and keywords.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The report is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. Your resume is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

Title: BibTeX Validator - Detect AI Hallucinations | Purplelink LLC

← All tools

Free web tool

# BibTeX Validator

Upload or paste a .bib file to check syntax, missing fields, dead DOIs, and verify your citations actually exist, including author and year correctness. Download a corrected .bib where CrossRef returns a confident match. Useful for catching AI-hallucinated references. Files are never stored.

Drag a .bib file here, or choose one. Max 2 MB.

Paste up to 2 MB of BibTeX directly. Same checks, no file needed.

Checks to run

Syntax & required fields (always on)

DOI resolution: verify each DOI is a live link

CrossRef: check titles exist in CrossRef (catches hallucinations)

Semantic Scholar: check titles in Semantic Scholar

Enabling DOI or database checks will send entry titles and authors to external services (doi.org, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar).

Files are never written to disk or logged.

## How to validate a BibTeX file online

- Upload your .bib file (drag-and-drop or click), or switch to Paste text and drop the BibTeX directly. Up to 2 MB.

- Syntax and required-field checks run automatically. Enable DOI resolution and/or CrossRef / Semantic Scholar checks to verify your citations actually exist (and that authors and years match).

- Click Validate .bib. A color-coded table shows each entry. Click any row to see the original BibTeX, plus the corrected version when CrossRef returned a confident match. Use the filter chips to focus on warnings or errors.

- Download the annotated .bib (your file with status comments) or the corrected .bib (entries rewritten from CrossRef metadata where confidence is high).

## About this tool

This tool validates BibTeX files in layers: syntax + completeness (always), DOI resolution (opt-in), and existence checks against CrossRef and Semantic Scholar (opt-in). When you enable the database checks, it also compares authors and publication years and can produce a corrected .bib for high-confidence matches. It's particularly useful for catching AI-hallucinated citations that have plausible-looking metadata but don't correspond to real papers.

Can it detect AI-hallucinated citations?

Yes. Enable the CrossRef and/or Semantic Scholar checks. For each entry with a title, the tool queries the database and reports how closely the title and author list match a real paper, and whether the year is off. Low-confidence title matches (below 50%) and author mismatches on otherwise-confident matches are flagged as likely hallucinations. For the full workflow and how the detection methods compare, see the guide on catching AI-hallucinated citations.

Are my files stored?

No. Your .bib file is validated in an ephemeral container and discarded immediately. When you enable DOI or database checks, titles and authors are sent to those external services. This is disclosed before you run the check.

What does the annotated .bib contain?

Your original .bib file with a comment line above each entry showing its validation status: missing required fields, DOI result, title and author confidence scores, and any year mismatch. Paste it straight back into your editor.

What is the corrected .bib?

For each entry where CrossRef returned a high-confidence match (title similarity at least 85%), the corrected .bib replaces the entry's fields with authoritative metadata: title, author list, year, DOI, journal or booktitle, volume, issue, pages, and publisher. Entries without a confident match are passed through unchanged. Each rewritten entry is marked with a "CORRECTED from CrossRef" comment so you can audit the changes.

How does the author check work?

Names are normalized to canonical last-name tokens (folding "John Smith", "Smith, John", "J. Smith", and "Müller" → "muller" all to the same key) and compared as a set against the authoritative author list. The score is the Jaccard overlap, so partial matches still get partial credit.

What BibTeX entry types are supported?

article, book, inproceedings, proceedings, phdthesis, mastersthesis, techreport, misc, incollection, inbook, booklet, manual, conference, unpublished, and thesis.

## The other kind of citation problem

A clean .bib fixes citations that are malformed. It cannot tell you about a citation that is well-formed and does not support the sentence attached to it. Paper Review reads it the way a referee would: four reviewer personas argue over the manuscript, every citation is checked against the live record, and figures are scanned for integrity problems. The report usually comes back in 4 to 8 minutes.

# Citation Generator

Enter a DOI, arXiv ID, or ISBN and get a formatted citation in four styles: APA 7th, MLA 9th, Chicago (author-date), and IEEE. Copy any of them with one click, or type the details in by hand.

DOI, arXiv ID, or ISBN

Before you submit, Paper Review (from $9) checks every reference in the manuscript against CrossRef.

DOI and ISBN lookups go directly from your browser to Crossref / Open Library. arXiv lookups relay through our server, since arXiv does not allow direct browser access. We never log or store anything you enter.

## How to generate a citation

- Paste a DOI, arXiv ID, or ISBN into the box (a doi.org or arxiv.org URL works too).

- Click Generate. Your browser looks the reference up and formats it in four styles.

- Click Copy on the style you need. Don't have an identifier? Use enter details manually instead.

- Proofread the result against your style guide. Automated metadata is good but not flawless.

## About this tool

This is a dependency-free citation generator. It resolves DOIs through Crossref, ISBNs through Open Library, and arXiv IDs through the arXiv API, then formats the metadata into APA 7th, MLA 9th, Chicago author-date, and IEEE styles entirely in your browser.

Which identifiers are supported?

DOIs (e.g. 10.1038/nphys1170 or a doi.org URL), arXiv IDs (e.g. 1706.03762 or an arxiv.org URL), and ISBN-10/13 (hyphens optional). You can also fill in the manual entry form for anything without an identifier, such as a website.

How accurate are the citations?

They are built from the metadata that Crossref or Open Library returns, which is usually accurate but occasionally incomplete or inconsistently capitalised. Treat the output as a strong draft and always check author order, title case, page ranges, and punctuation against your required style.

Why might an arXiv lookup fail?

Usually because the identifier doesn't match a paper on arXiv, or arXiv is briefly unreachable. If a lookup fails, the tool will tell you. Try the article's DOI instead (most arXiv papers have one once published), or use manual entry.

Is anything stored?

No. DOI and ISBN lookups go directly from your browser to the public APIs. arXiv lookups relay through our server, since arXiv doesn't allow direct browser access. All formatting happens locally either way, and we never log or store anything you enter.

# About Purplelink

Atlanta, Georgia · Founded 2026 · Georgia LLC

Purplelink LLC is a one-person software studio building Mac apps and manuscript tools for academic researchers, plus iOS apps for travel and health. The mission is simple: make software that solves real problems and lasts, not software that ships fast and deteriorates.

I'm Benjamin Ampel, a researcher in cybersecurity, AI and information systems, based in Atlanta. I've spent a lot of time in LaTeX: writing manuscripts, watching compile errors scroll by, checking references by hand before a deadline. The apps that stuck, for me, were always the ones that solved a specific problem I had, for people I understood. Purplelink is where I build those.

Source: https://purplelink.llc/guides/methodology-problems-peer-reviewers-flag/
Title: Methodology Problems Peer Reviewers Flag, and How to Fix Them | Purplelink LLC

← All guides

Guide

# Methodology problems peer reviewers flag, and how to fix them

By Benjamin Ampel · September 24, 2026

Many reviewer comments on empirical papers are not about the idea. They are about the distance between what a paper claims and what its methods can support. The same fifteen gaps come up again and again, and most of them have names. This guide defines each one, shows what it looks like on the page, and explains how to close it before a reviewer finds it.

Each section gives a one-sentence definition, why reviewers care, a sentence of the kind that draws the comment, and the fix. The example sentences are invented but typical. Primary literature is listed in the references, and each section links to a shorter explainer you can send to a co-author.

None of these problems means a paper is wrong. They mean it has not yet shown that it is right. Most can be fixed with an extra table, a clearer methods paragraph, or narrower wording in the abstract.

## Statistics and inference

The first four problems share a root. A p-value means what it claims only if the analysis was fixed before the data could influence it. Each is a different way the data ends up choosing the analysis.

### p-hacking

p-hacking is running several analyses of the same data and reporting the ones that reach statistical significance while leaving the others out.

Why reviewers care. A 5% significance threshold assumes one planned test. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn (2011) showed by simulation that a handful of ordinary, individually defensible choices (picking between two correlated outcome measures, adding participants after an early look, controlling for a covariate, dropping one condition) could together push the false-positive rate from 5% to more than 60%. Head et al. (2015) later found distributions of reported p-values across many fields that are consistent with p-hacking. Reviewers look for the traces: several p-values just under .05, measures in the methods that never reach the results, and covariates that appear in one model but not the next.

How it shows up. A results paragraph such as: Participants in the treatment condition reported higher satisfaction (p = .047); no significant differences emerged on the remaining measures, which are not discussed further. "Not discussed further" tells the reviewer other tests were run and set aside.

How to fix it. Decide the primary outcome and analysis before looking at the data, and write the decision down somewhere with a timestamp, such as a preregistration (Nosek et al., 2018). Report every measure, every condition and every exclusion, and if you excluded observations or added a covariate, also report the result without that choice, as Simmons and colleagues recommend. State how the sample size was decided, and label any unplanned analysis as exploratory.

Short explainer: p-hacking

### The garden of forking paths

The garden of forking paths is the set of reasonable, data-dependent analysis choices a researcher could have made, which inflates false positives even when only one analysis was actually run.

Why reviewers care. Gelman and Loken (2013) introduced the term to describe a problem that needs no fishing at all. A researcher runs one analysis in good faith, but the exclusion rule, the transformation, the subgroup and the covariate set were each chosen after seeing the data. Had the data come out differently, a different set of choices would have looked just as reasonable, so the single reported test carries the same inflated error rate as an explicit search (Gelman & Loken, 2014).

How it shows up. A methods sentence such as: Because reaction times were positively skewed, we log-transformed them and excluded trials more than 2.5 standard deviations from each participant's mean. Every clause is standard practice, but "because" signals that the choices followed the data.

How to fix it. Preregister the exclusion rules, transformations and covariates, or state that they follow an established lab or field convention and cite it. Where choices were made after seeing the data, show that they do not drive the result. A multiverse analysis reports the estimate under every reasonable combination of choices (Steegen et al., 2016), and a specification curve plots those estimates in order so the reader can see how many support the claim (Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson, 2020).

Short explainer: garden of forking paths

### HARKing

HARKing (hypothesizing after the results are known) is presenting a hypothesis that was formed after seeing the data as if it had been stated before the study began.

Why reviewers care. Kerr (1998) named the practice and set out its costs. A hypothesis suggested by a pattern in the data cannot fail a test on that same data, so the "confirmation" carries no evidential weight. It also hides the original hypothesis, which may have failed. Reviewers become suspicious when every prediction is confirmed, or when predictions are oddly specific, such as an effect in exactly one subgroup.

How it shows up. A results sentence such as: As predicted, the effect emerged only among participants high in need for cognition. If nothing earlier in the paper predicts that moderation, the reviewer will assume the prediction came after the finding.

How to fix it. Keep a dated record of your hypotheses before analysis; a preregistration is the most credible version. In the paper, separate confirmatory from exploratory results under their own headings. An unexpected finding is worth reporting, as long as it is reported as unexpected and framed as a hypothesis for future work. Some journals accept Registered Reports, in which the introduction and methods are reviewed and accepted in principle before data collection (Chambers, 2013).

Short explainer: HARKing

### Multiple comparisons

The multiple comparisons problem is that the chance of at least one false positive rises with every additional test run at the same significance threshold.

Why reviewers care. At α = .05, each test of a true null hypothesis has a 5% chance of a false positive. Across 20 independent tests, the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.9520, about 64%, and the expected number of false positives is one. Reviewers count the tests, including those implied by tables, and compare that number to the number of starred cells.

How it shows up. A sentence such as: We correlated each of the 12 personality facets with each of the 8 outcome measures; significant correlations are marked with an asterisk in Table 3. That is 96 tests; about five would reach p < .05 by chance.

How to fix it. Say how many tests you ran and apply a correction that fits your goal. To control the chance of any false positive (the familywise error rate), use Bonferroni or Holm's step-down procedure, which never rejects fewer hypotheses than Bonferroni (Holm, 1979). When you are screening many hypotheses and can tolerate a known proportion of false discoveries, control the false discovery rate with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Better still, designate a few primary comparisons in advance, so the correction applies to a short list.

Short explainer: multiple comparisons

## Samples and generalization

One of these limits what a study can detect; the other limits whom the findings apply to.

### Underpowered samples

An underpowered sample is one too small to reliably detect an effect of the size the authors consider meaningful.

Why reviewers care. Button et al. (2013) estimated the median statistical power of neuroscience studies at about 21% and explained why this matters even for positive results: when power is low, a significant finding is less likely to reflect a true effect, and the effect sizes that do reach significance tend to be overestimates. This follows from Ioannidis (2005), where the probability that a significant result is true depends on power, prior odds and bias. A reviewer who sees a small sample and a large effect reads the effect as a warning.

How it shows up. A pairing such as: The sample size was based on previous studies in this area. followed later by With 18 participants per group, the difference was significant (p = .03, d = 0.74), indicating a large effect of the intervention. The first is not a power analysis; the second is the pattern low power produces.

How to fix it. Justify the sample size before collecting data. A power analysis should state the smallest effect size you care about, where that number comes from, the planned test, alpha and target power, and the resulting N. Lakens (2022) covers this and other defensible justifications. If the data are already collected, report a sensitivity analysis: the smallest effect your design could detect with 80% power. Avoid "observed power" computed from your own effect estimate; it is a transformation of the p-value and adds no information (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001).

Short explainer: underpowered sample

### WEIRD samples

A WEIRD sample is drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic societies; the problem arises when findings from such a sample are presented as true of people in general.

Why reviewers care. Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) reviewed comparative evidence across domains including visual perception, fairness, cooperation, spatial reasoning and self-concept, and found that WEIRD participants were often outliers rather than typical humans. Susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion, for example, varies widely across societies. Arnett (2008) found that the great majority of participants in leading psychology journals came from the United States and a few other Western countries. A reviewer will check whether the abstract's claim is about the population sampled or about "people".

How it shows up. An abstract sentence such as: These results show that people rely on intuition rather than deliberation when making moral judgments. where the methods describe 240 undergraduates at one US university.

How to fix it. Report the sample's demographics in enough detail to judge its range. Match the wording of the conclusion to the population studied. Add a short statement of the constraints on generality, naming the populations, settings and materials to which you expect the result to extend and those to which you do not (Simons, Shoda & Lindsay, 2017). Where the claim needs to be universal, it needs data from more than one kind of society.

Short explainer: WEIRD samples

## Machine learning evaluation

Machine learning papers usually make a comparative claim: method A beats method B on benchmark C. Each of the next five problems weakens one part of that comparison.

### Test-train contamination

Test-train contamination occurs when examples from the evaluation set, or close copies of them, are present in the data a model was trained or tuned on, so the test measures memory rather than generalization.

Why reviewers care. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) documented data leakage across many scientific fields that use machine learning, including preprocessing fitted on the full dataset, duplicates across splits, and splits that ignore dependence between samples. For large language models the risk is larger, because pretraining corpora are huge and benchmarks are public. Brown et al. (2020) ran an n-gram overlap analysis between their pretraining data and each benchmark and reported the results; reviewers now expect something similar.

How it shows up. A methods sentence such as: We randomly split the 12,000 images into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. With several images per patient, the same patients land in both sets, and the model can score well by recognizing patients rather than disease.

How to fix it. Split by the unit you want to generalize to (patient, user, document, site or time period), not by row. Fit normalization, feature selection and any other preprocessing inside the training split only. Deduplicate across splits with a near-duplicate check, not just exact matching. For pretrained models, prefer benchmarks released after the training data cutoff, report an overlap check against whatever training data you can inspect, and compare scores on items flagged as possibly contaminated with scores on the rest.

Short explainer: test-train contamination

### Cherry-picked seeds

Cherry-picked seeds describes reporting a single training run, or the best of several, so that random run-to-run variation is presented as a difference between methods.

Why reviewers care. Random initialization, data order, data splits and nondeterministic hardware all move the final score. Henderson et al. (2018) showed in deep reinforcement learning that two groups of runs of the same algorithm, differing only in random seed, could produce results that looked like two different algorithms. Bouthillier et al. (2021) catalogued the sources of variance in machine learning benchmarks and recommended randomizing as many of them as possible across runs. If the gap between methods is smaller than the spread across seeds, a single number per method does not support a ranking.

How it shows up. A results sentence such as: Our method achieves 84.7% accuracy, a 0.6-point improvement over the strongest baseline (84.1%). with no mention of how many runs, no error bars, and the best number in each column in bold.

How to fix it. Run several seeds for every method, including baselines, and say how many. Report the mean with a standard deviation or confidence interval, and report all runs rather than the best. For comparisons across many tasks or with few runs, Agarwal et al. (2021) recommend interval estimates such as stratified bootstrap confidence intervals and robust aggregates such as the interquartile mean. If a single run is all you can afford, say so plainly and soften the claim.

Short explainer: cherry-picked seeds

### Hyperparameter asymmetry

Hyperparameter asymmetry is tuning the proposed method more thoroughly than the baselines it is compared against, so part of the reported gain comes from the extra tuning.

Why reviewers care. Re-evaluations have found that reported gains shrink or disappear once baselines get the same tuning effort. Melis, Dyer and Blunsom (2018) found that standard LSTMs, tuned with large-scale automatic search, outperformed more recent architectures on language modeling benchmarks. Lucic et al. (2018) found that with enough hyperparameter search and random restarts, most GAN variants reached similar scores, and no tested variant consistently beat the original. Dodge et al. (2019) showed that which model looks best can depend on the tuning budget, and proposed reporting expected validation performance as a function of that budget.

How it shows up. A methods sentence such as: Baselines were trained with the hyperparameters reported in their original papers; for our method, we selected the learning rate and dropout rate by grid search on the validation set.

How to fix it. Give every method the same search procedure and the same number of trials, over ranges that are reasonable for each. Use the same preprocessing, augmentation, training length and early-stopping rule. Report the search space, the budget and the selected values for every method in an appendix. If you copy baseline numbers from earlier papers, say so and explain why the setups are comparable.

Short explainer: hyperparameter asymmetry

### Missing ablations

A missing ablation is a proposed component whose individual contribution to the result was never tested by removing it and measuring the change.

Why reviewers care. If a paper introduces several changes at once, the combined result cannot show which one mattered. Lipton and Steinhardt (2019) listed "failure to identify the sources of empirical gains" among the troubling trends in machine learning scholarship, noting cases where gains attributed to a new architecture actually came from tuning or from a single small change.

How it shows up. A sentence such as: Combining the gated attention module, the curriculum schedule and the auxiliary contrastive loss, our model improves F1 by 3.2 points over the baseline. with no table showing what each of the three adds.

How to fix it. Add an ablation table. Each row removes one component, or adds one to the baseline, with everything else held fixed, including the tuning budget. Run ablation rows with the same number of seeds as the main results; otherwise small differences between rows are noise. Include the row a skeptic would ask for, usually the baseline plus only the simplest change. If a component does not help, drop it or say so.

Short explainer: missing ablations

### LLM self-judge bias

LLM self-judge bias is the tendency of a language model used as an evaluator to favor outputs from itself or its own model family, which inflates scores when the judge and the system under test are related.

Why reviewers care. Zheng et al. (2023) found that GPT-4's judgments agreed with human preferences at a rate similar to agreement between humans. They also documented position bias (favoring the first or second answer), verbosity bias (favoring longer answers) and self-enhancement bias (favoring its own answers), while noting that their evidence on the last was limited. Panickssery, Bowman and Feng (2024) found that models can recognize their own outputs and that this ability is linked to preferring them. When the judge is related to a system being compared, the reviewer cannot tell how much of the gap is the judge.

How it shows up. A methods sentence such as: Responses from our system and three baselines were rated for helpfulness on a 1 to 10 scale by the same model our system was fine-tuned from.

How to fix it. Use a judge from a different model family than any system under test, or several judges,. Collect human ratings on a random subset and report how well the judge agrees with them. In pairwise comparisons, present each pair in both orders. Report response length. Publish the judge prompt and the exact model version so the evaluation can be rerun.

Short explainer: LLM self-judge bias

## Reporting, citations and figures

These problems are not about the design of the study, but reviewers treat them as evidence of how carefully the rest was done.

### Hallucinated citations

A hallucinated citation is a reference that looks complete and plausible but does not correspond to a real publication, usually because it was produced by a generative AI tool.

Why reviewers care. Language models generate references by predicting plausible text, not by looking papers up. Walters and Wilder (2023) asked ChatGPT to write short literature reviews and checked every citation: 55% of the GPT-3.5 citations and 18% of the GPT-4 citations were fabricated, and many of the real ones contained errors. Some fabrications pair real authors with a title they never wrote, or attach a real DOI to the wrong paper. A reviewer who cannot find a key reference will wonder what else was not checked.

How it shows up. A sentence such as: Prior work has established that trust calibration improves human-AI team accuracy (Nguyen & Park, 2021). where the reference list gives a complete journal citation with volume, pages and DOI, and no such paper exists. (The citation here is invented to illustrate the pattern.)

How to fix it. Check every reference against a bibliographic database before submission: resolve each DOI and confirm that it lands on the paper you meant, and search each title in Crossref or Google Scholar. For the references that carry your main claims, open the source and confirm that it supports the sentence you attached it to. Remove anything you cannot find.

Short explainer: hallucinated citation

### Figure presentation

A figure presentation problem is a design choice in a chart, such as a truncated axis, missing or unlabeled error bars, or color-only encoding, that changes what a reader concludes from the data.

Why reviewers care. Weissgerber et al. (2015) showed that bar graphs of continuous data hide the distribution: very different datasets, including ones with outliers or bimodal groups, can produce identical bars. Crameri, Shephard and Heron (2020) showed that rainbow color maps distort data by creating false boundaries, and that they are hard to read for people with color-vision deficiency.

How it shows up. A text sentence such as: As Figure 3 shows, accuracy improved substantially in the treatment group. where Figure 3 is a bar chart with a y-axis running from 71% to 74%, six observations per group, and a caption reading only "Error bars show SE."

How to fix it. For small samples, plot individual observations, alone or over a box or violin plot. Start bar charts at zero; for small differences, use a dot plot instead of cropped bars. In every caption, state what the error bars represent (standard deviation, standard error or a confidence interval) and the n behind them. Use perceptually uniform color maps, and pair color with shape, line style or direct labels. Check that text is readable at the journal's column width.

Short explainer: figure presentation

## Study design and registration

The last two problems apply mostly to experiments with human or animal participants. In both cases a safeguard may well have been in place, but the manuscript does not give the reader enough to check it.

### Blinding not evidenced

Blinding not evidenced means a manuscript says a study was blinded without describing who was blinded, to what, and how the blinding was maintained.

Why reviewers care. Blinding protects against expectation effects in participants, in those delivering an intervention, and in those measuring outcomes. The word alone does not say which were covered. Schulz and Grimes (2002) pointed out that labels such as "double-blind" are used inconsistently and argued that authors should state exactly who was blinded. The CONSORT statement for randomized trials asks for who was blinded after assignment and how (Schulz, Altman & Moher, 2010), and the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines for animal research include blinding among their ten essential items (Percie du Sert et al., 2020).

How it shows up. A single methods sentence such as: All behavioral scoring was performed blind to genotype. with no detail about who held the key or when it was opened.

How to fix it. Name each group that was blinded: participants, experimenters, outcome assessors, data analysts. Say how allocation was concealed (who generated the codes, who held them, how samples or cages were labeled) and when the blind was broken relative to the analysis. If you tested whether blinding held, report the result. If blinding was not possible, say so, explain why, and describe what you did instead, such as using an objective outcome or an independent assessor.

Short explainer: blinding not evidenced

### Trial not registered

Trial not registered describes a clinical trial reported without a public registry entry made before the first participant enrolled, which leaves readers unable to check whether the reported outcomes were the planned ones.

Why reviewers care. In 2004 the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors announced that its member journals would consider a clinical trial only if it had been registered in a public registry, and for trials beginning enrollment after 1 July 2005, registered at or before the start of enrollment (De Angelis et al., 2004). The current ICMJE Recommendations keep the requirement and define a clinical trial broadly enough to include many behavioral interventions: any study that prospectively assigns people to an intervention to study its effect on a health outcome (ICMJE). Chan et al. (2004) compared trial protocols with the resulting publications and found that 62% of trials had at least one primary outcome that was changed, introduced or omitted.

How it shows up. A methods section that begins: Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention or to usual care, and the primary outcome was change in HbA1c at 12 weeks. with no registration number in the paper, or a registry entry that names 24 weeks, or one dated after enrollment began.

How to fix it. Register before the first participant enrolls and name the primary outcome and its time point precisely. Put the registry name and number in the abstract and methods. Make the reported primary outcome match the registered one. If it changed, report the change, when it was made and why. If a trial was registered late, say so rather than leaving the reviewer to find the date.

Short explainer: trial not registered

## Checking your own manuscript

The most reliable check is a colleague who knows your field and reads the manuscript as a skeptic. A useful way to brief them is to send this list and ask which of these a reviewer would raise.

If you want a first pass before that, Purplelink's Paper Review ($9) reads a manuscript PDF and reports methodology concerns in the terms used on this page. Several of these problems are flagged automatically, including hyperparameter asymmetry, missing sample-size justification, single-seed results, figure presentation problems and references that do not resolve, and findings link to the matching short explainer. It is advisory, it can be wrong, and it does not replace a person who knows your field. Its field profiles list what each one checks: machine learning, biomedicine, psychology and social science, and chemistry and materials.

For citations alone, the free BibTeX Validator checks each entry in a .bib file against CrossRef and Semantic Scholar and flags entries that do not match a real paper. It runs in your browser and does not upload the file.
