# How to Get Feedback on a Paper Before Submitting: Options Compared

By Benjamin Ampel · September 24, 2026

Colleagues, reading groups, writing centers, editing services, AI chat assistants, preprints and AI paper review tools compared on cost, turnaround, what each catches and what it misses.

The short answer: get one read from a person who knows your field, for framing and contribution, and one systematic check of methods, statistics, references, figures and formatting, which a structured tool or a paid service can do faster than a busy colleague.

No single option covers everything a journal reviewer will look at. A trusted colleague is the best judge of whether your contribution matters, and the worst person to ask to check 60 DOIs. An AI tool will check every reference in minutes and still miss that your framing ignores the debate your subfield has been having for three years. Below: what a pre-submission read should cover, how each option does, and a sequence that uses each for what it is good at.

I wrote this as the person who builds Paper Review, one of the options below. I have tried to describe it with the same plainness as the others, including what it does not do.

## What a pre-submission read should check

Whoever reads your draft, these are the things reviewers and editors most often raise. Use the list to decide which reader covers which item.

- Methods. Is the design able to answer the question you pose? Are baselines, controls and comparison conditions fair? Could someone replicate the procedure from what is written?

- Statistics. Is the sample size justified? Are multiple comparisons handled? Are effect sizes and uncertainty reported, not only p-values? The Why it matters series covers the common failures one by one.

- Claim-evidence alignment. Does the abstract say what the results tables show? "Outperforms" and "significantly" are the words that most often outrun the data.

- References that resolve. Every DOI should point to a real paper with the title you cite, and the cited source should say what you say it says. This matters more now that AI-drafted text can introduce plausible citations that do not exist.

- Figures. Readable axes, error bars where they belong, no truncated or broken scales that exaggerate a gap, and captions that match the plotted data.

- Anonymization. For double-blind venues: no author names, institutions, grant numbers, ethics protocol numbers, author-owned URLs or "in our previous work" self-citations left in the body.

- Journal compliance. Word and figure limits, required sections, data availability and reporting statements, reference style.

- Cover letter. A short, plain statement of what the paper contributes and why it fits this journal.

## The options compared

Costs and turnaround below are typical ranges, not quotes. Institutions and services vary, so treat them as a starting point.

Ways to get a critical read on a manuscript before submission

Option
Cost
Turnaround
What it catches well
What it misses
Confidentiality notes

Trusted colleague or advisor
Free in money; paid back in time and favors
Days to several weeks, depending on their load
Whether the contribution matters, framing, fit with the target venue, missing literature in your subfield
Often too busy for a line-by-line read; may be too close to the work or too polite; rarely checks every reference
High trust, informal. Fine for most work; get agreement first if co-authors or collaborators have constraints.

Internal lab or reading group
Free
Next scheduled meeting, usually one to two weeks
Unclear writing, confusing figures, gaps a smart outsider to the project notices, presentation of the argument
Depth on statistics unless a member specializes; systematic reference and formatting checks; group members share your blind spots
Stays inside the group. Circulate a fixed version so drafts do not spread.

University writing center
Usually free to enrolled students; availability for faculty and postdocs varies
Appointment-based, often within a week or two
Structure, clarity, paragraph flow, grammar, help for writers working in a second language
Consultants are often not specialists in your field, so methods and statistics are generally out of scope
Covered by the institution's policies. Ask how long drafts are kept if you upload files.

Professional language editing
Typically tens to a few hundred dollars, priced by word count
A few days to about a week; rush options cost more
Grammar, word choice, consistency, readability for an international audience
Not designed to judge methods, statistics or whether claims are supported
Reputable services have confidentiality terms. Read them, and check whether an editor or an AI system handles your file.

Paid "pre-submission peer review" service
Usually in the hundreds of dollars
Typically one to a few weeks
An outside expert-style report on methods, framing and journal fit, when the assigned reviewer knows your area
Quality depends heavily on who is assigned; may not verify every reference; slow if your deadline is close
Governed by the service's terms. Ask who reads the manuscript and whether they sign a confidentiality agreement.

Sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring and does not train on them. Purplelink deletes the manuscript and review 30 minutes after you first open the result, or after 24 hours.

## Where Paper Review fits, and where it doesn't

Paper Review is built for the systematic part of the checklist: the parts that are tedious for a person and easy to skip under deadline. You upload a PDF (up to 20 MB) and pick one of five domain profiles. A vision pass looks at every page for figure problems such as broken axes or missing error bars. Every reference is checked against CrossRef, and for the most load-bearing claims the cited source's abstract is fetched and compared to what you wrote. Four personas (Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic, Data Integrity Officer and Editor-in-Chief) read the paper in parallel, and findings raised independently by more than one of them are listed first. You get a Markdown report with an A/B/C rectification checklist, plus an annotated PDF with comments placed on the pages they refer to.

What it does not do matters as much. It will not tell you, the way a senior colleague can, that your framing misreads where the field is heading. It reads methods as written, so if the description is accurate and the analysis is wrong in code, it will not see that. Its citation check works at the abstract level, so a claim supported only in a paper's full text is marked "not supported by abstract" rather than wrong, and you have to check. Some findings will be mistaken. Each one quotes the passage it is about, so you can confirm or dismiss it quickly. The review is advisory; every decision stays with you. If a review reads as low quality, email within 14 days of purchase and the price is refunded.

## A workable sequence

For a paper you care about, spread the reads out so each one catches what the others miss.

- Four to six weeks out: a person who knows the field. Send your advisor, a co-author or a trusted colleague the draft with a specific question: "Is the contribution clear in the first two pages?" or "Is this the right venue?" Framing problems take the longest to fix, so find them first. A reading group session works well here too.

- Once the draft is close to final: a systematic check. Run Paper Review, with the Journal Pack if your target journal is supported. Work through the A items first. The walkthrough guide explains how to read each section of the report. If you only want a reference existence check, the free BibTeX Validator covers that part.

- If reviewers in your area are quick to say "you missed prior work": run Citation Gap Analysis ($3), which suggests papers an expert reviewer would expect you to cite. Treat each suggestion as a candidate to verify, since AI recall can be wrong.

- For double-blind venues, on the exact file you will upload: run Anonymity Check ($2). Paper Review includes an anonymity scan, but edits made after the review can reintroduce a name or a grant number, so check the final version. Still inspect figures, supplementary files and PDF metadata by hand. The double-blind guide lists what to strip.

- Last: the cover letter. Write it yourself or start from a draft with Cover Letter ($2), which works from your abstract and the journal name and never receives the full manuscript. See the cover letter guide.

When reviews come back, the same logic applies in reverse. How to respond to Reviewer 2 covers the reply, and Response to Reviewers ($6) checks whether your response letter addresses every comment and whether the revised manuscript contains the fixes you claim.

## Q&A

### When should I ask for feedback on a paper before submitting?

Ask a colleague or advisor for a read on framing and contribution four to six weeks before your target date, while there is still time to restructure. Run systematic checks on methods, statistics, references and formatting once the draft is close to final, and run a blinding check on the exact file you will upload.

### Can I paste my manuscript into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini for a review?

You can, and it will often produce useful comments on clarity and argument. It is less reliable for systematic work: long manuscripts can be read unevenly, references are not checked against a bibliographic database unless the assistant has a lookup tool and uses it for every entry, and whether your text may be used for model training depends on the product, the plan and your settings. Check those settings before pasting unpublished work.

### Is an AI paper review tool a substitute for a domain expert?

No. An AI review can check a manuscript systematically and quickly, but it cannot tell you with an expert's confidence whether the contribution matters to your subfield, and it can be wrong. Use it alongside at least one human reader who knows the area.

### What happens to my manuscript if I use Purplelink Paper Review?

The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API for analysis. Anthropic retains inputs for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring and does not use them for model training. Purplelink deletes the manuscript and the review from its servers 30 minutes after you first open the result, or after 24 hours if you never do, so save the report before closing the tab. Redact identifiable patient data before uploading.

### Does posting a preprint count as getting feedback?

Sometimes. A preprint on arXiv, SSRN or OSF can attract comments, but many preprints receive few or none, and the manuscript becomes public. Check the target journal's preprint policy first, and for double-blind venues check whether a public preprint is allowed and how it should be handled.

Title: Can You Use AI to Check Your Own Manuscript? What Publisher Policies Say | Purplelink

# Can You Use AI to Check Your Own Manuscript? What Publisher Policies Say

By Benjamin Ampel · September 24, 2026

What ten publisher and venue policies say about authors using AI tools on their own manuscript before submission, what has to be disclosed and where, and why the upload ban you have heard about applies to reviewers.

The short answer: yes. Every major publisher and venue policy we checked allows authors to use AI tools while preparing a manuscript. They add three conditions: an AI tool cannot be listed as an author, you stay responsible for everything in the paper, and some uses have to be disclosed. The rule that bans uploading manuscripts to AI is aimed at reviewers, who hold someone else's unpublished work in confidence. It is not about authors checking their own.

Policies change, and each journal can add its own rules on top of its publisher's. Treat this page as a map, then read the policy for your target venue. Every row in the table below links to it. Checked September 2026.

I build Paper Review, an AI pre-submission review, so I have a stake in the answer. I have tried to report what the policies say, including the parts that ask something of you.

## Where the confusion comes from

Most researchers first meet an AI rule as a reviewer: "do not upload the manuscript you are reviewing to ChatGPT." That rule is about confidentiality. A reviewer has been trusted with someone else's unpublished work and has no right to pass it to a third party. Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, IEEE, ACM and ICMJE all have a version of it.

The author's situation is different. The work is yours, and whether to share it is your decision. The author-side policies therefore ask different questions: did AI write part of the paper, is it disclosed, and does the tool you used keep your unpublished work confidential?

## What the policies say, by publisher and venue

Summaries in my words. Where a column says "check the page", the policy was not clear enough for me to summarize it confidently.

Author-side generative AI rules, September 2026

Publisher or venue
May authors use AI?
Where to disclose

Elsevier

## What they agree on

- AI is never an author. Every policy that addresses authorship says so, for the same reason: authorship means accountability, and a tool cannot be accountable.

- You own every claim. Text, numbers, citations and figures are the authors' responsibility whether or not a tool helped produce them. A citation an AI invented is your fabricated citation.

- Disclosure follows content, not contact. The trigger is AI that generated or substantively changed what is in the paper, or AI used in the research itself. Most policies exempt grammar and copy editing. Where the disclosure goes differs, so follow your venue's instructions.

- Check the tool's terms. Elsevier, Wiley and Taylor & Francis ask authors to make sure a tool keeps unpublished work confidential and does not gain the right to train on it. ACM, ICMJE and ICML frame their rules around whether confidentiality is assured, too.

## Does a critique of your draft need disclosing?

None of the policies above addresses this case directly. A tool that reads your manuscript and reports problems, without writing any text that ends up in the paper, is closer to a colleague's read than to a writing assistant. By the disclosure triggers above (generated or substantively changed content), feedback alone does not obviously require a statement.

That is my reading, not policy text. If your venue's rules are strict or unclear, a one-line note costs nothing: "The authors used an AI review tool to check the manuscript for errors before submission; all changes were made by the authors." If you then rewrite a section using text the tool suggested, that part falls under the ordinary disclosure rules.

Venues are moving in this direction themselves. For ICML 2026, the conference offered authors an optional program of automated pre-submission feedback on their manuscripts, kept private from reviewers, and ICLR has announced the same for its submitters.

## A checklist before you upload your own manuscript

- Read the tool's data terms. Where does the file go, who processes it, how long is it kept, and can it be used for training? Consumer chat apps differ by plan and setting; API and enterprise terms are usually stricter.

- Check co-authors agree. The manuscript belongs to all of them.

- Remove what should not leave your hands. Identifiable patient or participant data, embargoed results, and anything a data use agreement restricts.

- Verify what comes back. Treat every finding as a claim to check, especially suggested references.

- Disclose if you used generated text. Follow the target venue's instructions for where and how.

## How Paper Review handles your manuscript

For comparison against the checklist: Paper Review sends the manuscript to Anthropic's Claude API for analysis. Under Anthropic's commercial terms, inputs are retained for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring and are not used for model training. Reference titles and DOIs are sent to CrossRef to check that they exist. Purplelink deletes the manuscript and the review from its servers 30 minutes after you first open the result, or after 24 hours if you never do. The review writes nothing into your paper: it quotes your passages and lists what to check, and every change is yours. There is no account, and the privacy policy has the full detail.

## Q&A

### Can I use ChatGPT or Claude to check my paper before submitting to an Elsevier or Springer Nature journal?

Both publishers allow authors to use AI tools while preparing a manuscript, provided the authors stay responsible for the content and disclose AI-generated or substantively edited text as each policy describes. The restriction on uploading manuscripts to AI applies to reviewers. Check the tool's data terms before uploading unpublished work.

### Why can't reviewers use AI on the manuscript when authors can?

Because the reviewer is holding someone else's confidential, unpublished work. Sharing it with a third-party tool is the reviewer's decision to make about another person's paper. An author sharing their own manuscript is making that decision about their own work.

### Do I need to disclose that I used an AI tool to proofread my paper?

Usually not. Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, ACM and NeurIPS exempt spelling, grammar or copy editing, and IEEE treats it as generally outside its policy while recommending disclosure. Some bodies state no exemption, so check your venue's page.

### Can an AI tool be listed as a co-author?

No. Every publisher and venue policy that addresses authorship rules it out, because an AI tool cannot take responsibility for the work.

# Overleaf alternative for Mac: offline LaTeX editors compared

By Benjamin Ampel · September 24, 2026

The best Overleaf alternative on a Mac is a local TeX distribution (MacTeX or TinyTeX) plus a native editor: TeXShop if you want free and standard, Texifier or ModernTex if you want a modern paid Mac app, and Overleaf itself for any draft that co-authors edit at the same time.

Disclosure up front: Purplelink makes ModernTex, one of the editors compared here. I have tried to write this the way I would want to read it: Overleaf is the right tool for a lot of work, and the free options below are good enough for most people. ModernTex's entry sticks to what the app does today, including what it does not do.

## When Overleaf is the right choice

People go looking for an Overleaf alternative after a slow compile, a timeout on the free tier, or a flight with no Wi-Fi. Before you switch, it is worth being clear about what Overleaf does better than anything you can install.

- Real-time collaboration. Several people can type in the same document at once and see each other's cursors, with comments and tracked changes alongside. No desktop LaTeX editor does this as well. If your paper has four co-authors editing the methods section in the week before a deadline, that is Overleaf's job.

- Zero install. Overleaf runs the TeX distribution on its own servers. Nothing to download, no 5 GB MacTeX package, nothing to update. It also means a co-author on Windows, a student on a Chromebook and you on a Mac all compile with the same setup.

- Institutional licences. Many universities pay for Overleaf through a site licence, which gives everyone on campus the premium features. If yours does, the usual free-tier complaints (compile time limits, collaborator caps, no Git) may not apply to you at all.

- Journal templates. The template gallery is large, and some publishers link to their Overleaf template directly from their author instructions.

If you mostly co-author, and you are always online, you may not need an alternative. What follows is for everyone else.

## What you gain and give up by going local

Writing LaTeX on your own Mac changes a few concrete things.

You gain:

- Offline work. The distribution and the editor are on your disk. Trains, planes and bad conference Wi-Fi stop mattering.

- No compile limits. A long thesis with many figures compiles for as long as it needs to. On a recent Mac, local compiles are usually quick.

- Your files, on your disk. The project is a folder of ordinary files. You can back it up, version it with Git, or keep sensitive material (unpublished data, reviewer identities, embargoed results) off a third-party server.

- A native app. Mac keyboard shortcuts, system spell-check, dark mode, and a window that behaves like every other window on your machine.

You give up:

- Live co-editing. Nothing on this list matches Overleaf for several people in one document at once.

- The zero-setup start. You install a TeX distribution and keep it updated, roughly once a year when a new TeX Live ships.

- Identical builds for everyone. Your TeX Live year, fonts and settings are yours, so a co-author's machine can behave slightly differently.

## The options, compared

Every local option needs a TeX distribution installed separately, except where the table says otherwise. "Synced PDF preview" means clicking in the source jumps to the matching spot in the PDF and back, which in most editors is done through SyncTeX. "BibTeX completion" means the editor suggests citation keys from your .bib file as you type \cite{.

### TeXShop

TeXShop ships inside MacTeX, so if you have installed MacTeX you already have it. Source on one side, PDF on the other, a Typeset button, and SyncTeX in both directions. It has been maintained for over twenty years and nearly every Mac LaTeX tutorial assumes it. What it lacks is polish: the interface is dated, and there is no built-in citation search. Choose it if you want a free, dependable default and do not mind plain.

### TeXstudio

TeXstudio is free, open source and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It has more built in than TeXShop: a structure panel, completion for commands, labels and citation keys, table and figure wizards, and an error list you can click through. It is a cross-platform Qt app, so menus and shortcuts do not follow Mac conventions. Choose it if you also work on a Windows or Linux machine and want the same editor on each.

### Texifier (formerly Texpad)

Texifier is the established paid native Mac editor, with an iOS app for writing on an iPad. It can typeset as you type and does not require a separate MacTeX install, which makes it the smoothest move for someone leaving Overleaf who does not want to manage a distribution. It is a one-time purchase rather than a subscription; check the developer's site for the current price. Choose it if you want a polished Mac app and an iPad companion.

### VS Code with LaTeX Workshop

If you already write code in VS Code, the LaTeX Workshop extension turns it into a capable LaTeX setup: build recipes, an embedded PDF viewer with SyncTeX, citation completion and Git in the sidebar. Microsoft's Live Share extension lets a co-author join a live editing session, which is the closest a desktop editor gets to Overleaf, though it is a session you host rather than a shared document that is always there. Choose it if VS Code is already open all day.

### Emacs with AUCTeX, or Vim with VimTeX

Both are free, run anywhere, and are among the most capable LaTeX environments available, with project-aware citation lookup and inverse search through a Mac PDF viewer such as Skim. The price is the learning curve of the editor itself. Choose one if you already use it for everything else.

### ModernTex

ModernTex is the native macOS LaTeX editor we make, built for journal articles, conference papers and dissertation chapters rather than general-purpose editing. It handles multi-file manuscripts with root file detection, keeps the PDF in sync in both directions, completes citations by searching your .bib by author or title, and explains compile errors in plain language. It also has submission-readiness checks (anonymization, page limits, required sections), an anonymized export for double-blind review, version snapshots, and visual editors for TikZ figures and tables that write the LaTeX for you.

What it does not do: real-time collaboration. It is a single-user app, and two people cannot type in the same file at once. It runs only on macOS 14 or later, has no iPad app, and it is new, first released in 2026, so it has far less of a track record than TeXShop or Texifier. It needs a TeX distribution; if none is found when you compile, it offers to install TinyTeX for you. Choose it if you write manuscripts alone on a Mac and the submission-focused features are the ones you keep wishing for. The trial is the full app for seven days, and keeping it is $10 once.

## How to move a project from Overleaf to a Mac editor

A LaTeX project is portable by design, so the move takes minutes. Most of the work is matching the settings Overleaf chose for you.

- Download the source. In the Overleaf editor, open the Menu and choose Download > Source. You get a zip of every file in the project. Unzip it into a folder you will keep, not your Downloads folder.

- Install a TeX distribution. MacTeX is the full TeX Live for macOS, about 5 GB, and includes every package a template is likely to load. TinyTeX and BasicTeX are far smaller and add packages as you need them with tlmgr install. If disk space is not a problem, MacTeX saves you a round of "file not found" errors.

- Note Overleaf's settings before you leave. In the Overleaf Menu, check the Compiler (pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX) and the Main document. Set the same compiler in your editor, and open the same main .tex file, or mark it as the root file.

- Check the bibliography tool. Overleaf runs latexmk, which picks BibTeX or Biber automatically. If your preamble loads biblatex, your editor needs to run Biber; if it uses \bibliography{} with a .bst style, BibTeX. Most editors can run latexmk too, which removes the guesswork.

- Enable shell escape if you need it. Overleaf compiles with shell escape on, so packages such as minted or some svg workflows just work there. Locally they fail until you add -shell-escape to the compile command. Turn it on only for projects that need it.

- Check fonts under XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX. A fontspec line that names a font works only if that font is installed on your Mac. Overleaf's servers have a different font set from macOS, so install the font or switch to one you have.

- Compile and compare. Build once and compare the PDF against the last Overleaf PDF. Page count and reference list are the quickest checks.

If you are on a machine without a TeX install and need one PDF today, our LaTeX to PDF tool compiles a project in the browser; this guide covers multi-file projects.

## Keep Overleaf for collaboration, edit locally

Many research groups do not choose one or the other. They keep the shared draft on Overleaf, where co-authors comment and edit, and each person who prefers a local editor works on a copy on their own machine.

The clean way to do this is Git. Overleaf offers Git integration (clone the project with git, edit locally, push back) and GitHub sync (link the project to a GitHub repository). Both are premium features: they are available on Overleaf's paid plans and through many institutional licences, not on the free tier. Check your account before you plan around them.

A few habits keep this working:

- Pull before you start, push when you stop. If a co-author edits the same lines on Overleaf while you edit locally, Git will ask you to resolve a conflict. Short sessions and frequent pushes keep conflicts rare.

- Agree on one main file and one compiler. Everyone should build the same way, or someone's PDF will differ.

- Leave generated files out. Commit .tex, .bib, images and class files. Keep .aux, .log, .bbl and the PDF out of the repository with a .gitignore.

- Sections you own are easiest. If each author writes in their own \input file, local editing and live editing rarely collide.

On a free Overleaf account, the fallback is manual: download the source, edit locally, then upload the changed files back, replacing the old versions. It works for occasional use, but it is easy to overwrite a co-author's edit, so tell them first. Any local editor on this page, including ModernTex, fits this workflow, since each one edits ordinary files in a folder.

## Which to choose

- Co-authors edit at the same time? Keep Overleaf, at least for the shared draft.

- Want free and standard on a Mac? TeXShop.

- Also use Windows or Linux? TeXstudio.

- Want a polished Mac app with an iPad version? Texifier.

- Already live in VS Code, Emacs or Vim? Stay there and add the LaTeX extension.

- Writing papers alone on a Mac and want help getting them submission-ready? ModernTex, $10 once.

For a longer look at fourteen Mac editors, including Octree, Texmaker, LyX and others not covered here, see the best LaTeX editors for Mac.

## Frequently asked questions

Is there an offline version of Overleaf for Mac?

No. Overleaf is a web app and there is no Overleaf desktop app for macOS. Overleaf does publish an open-source Community Edition that a lab or department can host on its own server, but that is still a website. Writing LaTeX offline on a Mac means installing a TeX distribution such as MacTeX or TinyTeX and using a local editor.

What is the best free Overleaf alternative for Mac?

TeXShop, for most people. It is free, it installs with MacTeX, and it has a synced PDF preview. TeXstudio is the free choice if you also work on Windows or Linux, and VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension is the free choice if you already write code in VS Code.

Can I keep using Overleaf with co-authors and edit on my Mac?

Yes. The project is the same set of .tex, .bib and image files either way. Overleaf's Git integration and GitHub sync let you pull the project to your Mac, edit locally and push back, but both are premium features, available on paid plans and through many institutional licences. On a free account you can download the source as a zip and upload changed files by hand.

Will my Overleaf project compile the same way on my Mac?

Usually, once you match three settings. Use the same compiler Overleaf used (pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX), run Biber if the project uses biblatex, and enable shell escape if it uses packages such as minted. Fonts called by name under XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX must also be installed on the Mac.

Does ModernTex have real-time collaboration like Overleaf?

No. ModernTex is a single-user Mac app. Your files are ordinary files on disk, so you can share them through whatever you already use, but two people cannot type in the same document at the same time. If you need that, keep Overleaf for the shared draft.

Do I need the full 5 GB MacTeX install?

No. BasicTeX and TinyTeX are much smaller and install missing packages on demand with tlmgr. Full MacTeX is the easiest option if you have the disk space, because every package a template might load is already there.

Title: Best LaTeX editor for Mac in 2026: 14 editors compared | Purplelink

Comparison

# Best LaTeX editor for Mac in 2026: 14 editors compared

By Benjamin Ampel · May 31, 2026, updated September 11, 2026

A direct comparison of the LaTeX editors that actually work on Mac in 2026, covering what each one is good at, what it costs, and which workflow it suits. No affiliate links, no rankings padding.

Disclosure up front: I make one of the editors on this list (ModernTex). I've tried to write the comparison honestly. TeXShop is the right call for most academics today, and Texifier is the right call for most people who want a polished modern editor. ModernTex shipped its 1.0 in September 2026; I've kept its entry to what the app actually does today.

## What you actually need to run LaTeX on a Mac

A LaTeX editor is only half of the setup, and this trips up most people
coming to LaTeX on a Mac for the first time. You need two things:

- A TeX distribution. This is the engine that turns your
.tex source into a PDF. On macOS that is almost always MacTeX,
which bundles the TeX Live distribution with a few Mac-specific
applications. It is a large download, around 5 GB, because it ships
every package you might ever cite.

- An editor. This is where you write. It sends your file
to the distribution, shows you the resulting PDF, and tells you what went
wrong when the compile fails. This is the part you get to choose, and it is
what the rest of this page compares.

The distinction matters because a lot of "LaTeX won't work on my Mac"
problems are really "no TeX distribution is installed". If you open a
.tex file and nothing compiles, install MacTeX first and then
pick an editor. The one exception is Overleaf, which runs the distribution on
its own servers, so nothing is installed locally at all.

macOS does not include a TeX distribution, and neither Pages nor TextEdit
will compile LaTeX. There is no built-in option the way there is for Markdown
previewing.

## The shortlist

- TeXShop: free, ships with MacTeX, the default for most academics.

- Texifier (formerly Texpad): paid, polished, modern Mac native.

- Octree: free, AI-assisted, web-based with Mac wrapper.

- VS Code + LaTeX Workshop: free, general-purpose code editor with a strong LaTeX extension.

- Overleaf: web-based, collaborative, runs in any browser.

- ModernTex: $10, native macOS, focused on the academic manuscript workflow.

Those six are the ones worth a real look. Eight more that run on a Mac are covered further down, including TeXstudio and Texmaker, with a straight answer on why each is not on the shortlist.

## TeXShop

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS-only. Installed by: almost every academic with a Mac and MacTeX.

TeXShop is the editor that ships with the MacTeX distribution. It's been around for over 20 years, it's actively maintained by Richard Koch at the University of Oregon, and it does one thing well: edit a .tex file and compile it with whatever engine MacTeX provides. Side-by-side editor and PDF preview, SyncTeX click-to-source, basic syntax highlighting, multi-file support via root document declaration.

What it's good at: reliability. Compatible with every TeX distribution macro you'll encounter. No telemetry, no cloud, no subscription. If a tutorial says "open TeXShop and...", that's a feature.

What it lacks: modern UX (the interface looks like 2010), no inline BibTeX autocomplete, no plain-language error messages, no built-in tracked-changes view. Searching across a multi-file project is functional but not great.

Pick TeXShop if you want the closest thing to a default and you don't mind the dated interface. Most senior researchers do, in fact, pick TeXShop.

## Texifier (formerly Texpad)

Cost: $29.99 (occasional discount). Platform: macOS + iOS.

Texifier is the polished Mac-native option that most people who actually shop for a LaTeX editor end up with. It bundles its own TeX distribution (no MacTeX install required), has incremental typesetting (PDF updates as you type with no manual compile), a structure sidebar that maps your manuscript by sections, and the best autocomplete-for-LaTeX experience available.

What it's good at: the "it just works" experience. Outline sidebar makes navigating a long manuscript feel natural. iPad app is genuinely usable. Active development.

What it lacks: deep bibliography tooling. The BibTeX autocomplete is good but not specifically built for academic writing workflows. Tracked-changes via latexdiff requires external tools.

Pick Texifier if you want a polished, modern Mac-native experience and you're willing to pay $30 for it. This is the right answer for most working researchers writing journal-length manuscripts on a Mac today.

## Octree

Cost: Free tier with limits, paid plan ~$10/mo. Platform: Web + Mac wrapper.

The newer entrant. AI-assisted writing (suggestions, grammar, rewrites) on top of a competent LaTeX editor. The cloud-first design is a real distinguishing feature, because your project lives on Octree's servers, accessible from any device.

What it's good at: AI-assisted drafting. If you want copilot-style suggestions while you write, Octree is the only mainstream option that integrates them well.

What it lacks: on-device privacy. Your manuscript is on Octree's servers by default. For sensitive research (medical, military, IP), that's disqualifying.

Pick Octree if AI-assisted writing is core to your workflow and your research isn't sensitive. Avoid if "no cloud" is a requirement.

## VS Code + LaTeX Workshop

Cost: Free. Platform: cross-platform.

If you're a developer who also writes academic papers, VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension is the path of least resistance. Build chains are configurable, snippets are mature, Git integration is the same as your code projects. SyncTeX preview works well.

What it's good at: consistency with the rest of your toolchain if you spend most of your day in VS Code. Free, extensible, version-controllable settings.

What it lacks: a manuscript-first feel. VS Code is a code editor, so the document feels like a code file, not like a paper. Outline navigation works but isn't built for chapters and bibliographies.

Pick VS Code if you already live in VS Code and want one less context switch.

## Overleaf

Cost: Free tier (limited compile time, no Git sync), paid plans $15–$25/mo.

Browser-based, collaborative. Overleaf is the de facto choice for multi-author papers where co-authors aren't all comfortable installing LaTeX. The collaboration model (Google Docs-style) works.

What it's good at: multi-author collaboration. Templates for major journals. No local install required.

What it lacks: offline access on the free tier, Git sync on free, native-Mac feel. The editor itself runs in a browser.

Pick Overleaf if you need real-time collaboration. Many academic teams use Overleaf for collaboration and a native editor for solo writing.

## ModernTex

Cost: $10, one-time, every 1.x update included, after a free 7-day trial. Platform: macOS 14+. Status: shipping, version 1.0 released September 2026.

I built ModernTex specifically because the existing options miss a few things that matter for academic manuscript work: plain-language compile error explanations (BibTeX-style cryptic errors are the #1 frustration for new users), BibTeX autocomplete that searches by author or title across your entire .bib, revision snapshots tied to ideas not files, submission-readiness checks that catch journal-specific issues before you upload, and a live TikZ figure editor for building flowcharts and diagrams by dragging boxes instead of writing coordinates by hand.

Why a new editor when Texifier exists: Texifier is excellent but optimizes for general LaTeX users (programmers, technical writers, students). ModernTex narrows the focus to academic manuscript writers, the workflow of writing a journal article or dissertation chapter, from outline to camera-ready. That's a deliberate constraint.

What it lacks: a track record. Version 1.0 shipped in September 2026, so it has none of the twenty years of edge-case coverage TeXShop has, and no iPad app. It also needs a TeX distribution installed; it does not bundle one the way Texifier does.

Pick ModernTex if you write journal articles or dissertation chapters on a Mac and the manuscript-first features above are what you keep wishing for. The trial is free for seven days; keeping it is $10, once.

## Eight more LaTeX editors that run on a Mac

Every one of these works on macOS today. They are not on the shortlist because, for someone choosing an editor on a Mac in 2026, each is beaten by one of the six above at the thing it is best at. The exception is TeXstudio, which is the right answer for a specific person: anyone who also works on Windows or Linux.

### TeXstudio

Cost: Free, open source. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

The most widely installed LaTeX editor that is not tied to one platform. It began as a fork of Texmaker and has grown well past it: an integrated PDF viewer with SyncTeX, a structure panel for long documents, autocomplete for commands and references, wizards for tables and figures, spell-checking as you type. It is a Qt application, so it does not look or behave like a Mac app. Menus, shortcuts and dialogs feel like they were designed elsewhere, because they were.

Pick TeXstudio if you move between a Mac and a Windows or Linux machine and want the identical editor on both. If you only write on a Mac, TeXShop does the same job and feels native.

### Texmaker

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

The editor TeXstudio was forked from, still maintained by its original author, and simpler for it: built-in PDF viewer, SyncTeX, Unicode, spell-check, code folding, and less of everything else. If you opened TeXstudio and found it busy, this is the same idea with fewer panels.

Pick Texmaker if you want a cross-platform editor and TeXstudio felt like too much. Otherwise the same advice applies: on a Mac alone, TeXShop.

### TeXworks

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux. Installed by: you, already, if you installed MacTeX.

TeXworks ships inside MacTeX and TeX Live, and was deliberately modelled on TeXShop's simplicity so that other platforms would have something like it. Source window, PDF window, SyncTeX, a typeset button. That is the whole editor. It is fine for a first document and you will outgrow it by the second chapter.

Pick TeXworks if it is already on your machine and you need to compile something today. Then pick something else.

### LyX

Cost: Free, open source. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

LyX is not a LaTeX editor in the sense of the rest of this page. It is a document processor that generates LaTeX for you: you work in a structured, roughly formatted view and rarely see a backslash. For a thesis written alone, where you never need to hand a .tex file to anyone, that can be pleasant. The moment a journal template, a co-author, or a fussy figure needs raw LaTeX, you are fighting the tool. It still needs a TeX distribution installed.

Pick LyX if you want LaTeX output without writing LaTeX and will never share source. Most academics eventually need to share source.

### Archimedes

Cost: Paid, one-time. Platform: macOS, with an iOS version.

A native Mac editor for Markdown with LaTeX math, with live preview and a math-focused toolbar. It is built for writing notes, problem sets and math-heavy documents, not for compiling a full journal manuscript with a bibliography and a class file. Good at what it is for, which is not what most of this page's readers are doing.

Pick Archimedes if your LaTeX is mostly equations inside otherwise plain documents. For a paper, use one of the six above.

### TeX64

Cost: Paid. Platform: macOS.

A newer native macOS editor that compiles locally through the MacTeX or TeX Live installation you already have, rather than bundling its own distribution the way Texifier does. It is recent enough that I would not yet rely on it for a deadline, for the same reason I say that about ModernTex: no track record. Worth watching if native-Mac matters to you and you already have MacTeX installed.

Pick TeX64 if you want a native app, do not want a second TeX distribution on disk, and are comfortable being an early adopter.

### Emacs with AUCTeX

Cost: Free. Platform: anything.

AUCTeX plus RefTeX is, feature for feature, one of the most capable LaTeX environments that exists: inline previews of equations, cross-reference and citation lookup that understands your whole project, folding, and a compile loop you can bend to any shape. The learning curve is the entire Emacs learning curve. If you already live in Emacs you know this and did not need this page. If you do not, this is not the week to start.

Pick AUCTeX if you are already an Emacs user. Nobody else.

### Neovim or Vim with VimTeX

Cost: Free. Platform: anything.

VimTeX is excellent: compilation, syntax, text objects for environments and commands, folding, and forward and inverse search when paired with a PDF viewer such as Skim on the Mac. The same caveat as Emacs applies. It rewards people who already think in Vim and punishes everyone else.

Pick VimTeX if Vim is already how you write everything. Otherwise VS Code with LaTeX Workshop gives you most of the benefit with none of the modal editing.

Sublime Text with the LaTeXTools package and BBEdit with its TeX syntax highlighting also exist. Neither adds anything the eight above do not, so they are not covered separately.

## Decision matrix

- Want the default? TeXShop.

- Want polished and modern, willing to pay? Texifier.

- Want AI-assisted drafting? Octree.

- Already in VS Code? VS Code + LaTeX Workshop.

- Need real-time collaboration? Overleaf.

- Academic manuscripts on macOS as your dominant use case? ModernTex, $10.

- Also work on Windows or Linux? TeXstudio.

- Already live in Emacs or Vim? AUCTeX or VimTeX. You knew that.

## Installing LaTeX on a Mac: MacTeX, BasicTeX, or Overleaf

Whichever editor you land on, the install order is the same: distribution
first, editor second. And "MacTeX vs Overleaf" is not really an either-or.
One is a distribution you install, the other is a website that installs
nothing. The question is whether you want LaTeX on your own machine.
If you are weighing that move, Overleaf
alternatives for Mac covers what you give up and how to move a project.

MacTeX is the standard choice. Download the package from
the TeX Users Group, run the installer, and you have TeX Live plus TeXShop,
BibDesk and LaTeXiT. It is about 5 GB installed. Nearly every tutorial
you will read assumes this is what you have, which is a real advantage when
something breaks at 11pm before a deadline.

BasicTeX is the same distribution trimmed to roughly
100 MB. It omits most packages, so you install them individually with
tlmgr as documents demand them. Worth it if disk space is tight,
painful if you are new, because a missing package surfaces as a compile error
rather than a prompt.

Homebrew works too, via brew install --cask
mactex or mactex-no-gui. Same distribution, managed
alongside your other packages.

Installing nothing is also an option. Overleaf runs entirely in the browser.
For a single co-authored paper on a borrowed machine that is often the right
answer, and you can move to a local setup later without changing your source
files. Our LaTeX to PDF compiler will also
build a document without any local install if you just need one PDF.

Apple Silicon no longer needs any special handling. MacTeX has shipped native
arm64 binaries for years, and every editor on this page runs natively on M
series hardware.

### Which LaTeX compiler to use on a Mac

People search for the best LaTeX compiler for Mac, and the honest answer is
that it is not a Mac question. MacTeX ships all three engines you would ever
choose between, and every editor above lets you pick. pdfLaTeX
is the default, the fastest, and what nearly every journal template assumes;
start there. XeLaTeX adds system fonts and proper Unicode,
which matters for non-Latin scripts or a document that must use a specific
typeface. LuaLaTeX does what XeLaTeX does and is where newer
packages are heading. Switch engines only when a package or a font forces
you to, not because one is "best".

## Frequently asked

### Is there a free LaTeX editor for Mac?

Yes, several. TeXShop is free and arrives with MacTeX, so most people
already have it. VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension is free. Overleaf
has a free tier with limits on compile time and no Git sync. Of the paid
options, Texifier is a one-time $29.99 rather than a subscription.

### Does macOS come with LaTeX?

No. macOS ships no TeX distribution and no LaTeX editor. You need to
install MacTeX, or use a browser-based option like Overleaf.

### What is the difference between a LaTeX editor and a TeX distribution?

The distribution compiles your document. The editor is where you write it
and read the errors. MacTeX is a distribution, TeXShop and Texifier are
editors. You need one of each, except with Overleaf, which provides both.

### Which LaTeX editor is best for academic writing on a Mac?

For most researchers today, Texifier if you will pay for polish, TeXShop if
you want the default that every tutorial assumes. Choose Overleaf instead when
co-authors need to edit the same file at the same time.

### Is TeXstudio available for Mac?

Yes. TeXstudio runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and is free. It is the best
choice if you also work on another platform. On a Mac alone, TeXShop does the
same job and feels like a Mac app, which TeXstudio does not.

### MacTeX or Overleaf?

MacTeX if you want LaTeX on your own machine: it works offline, compiles
faster on any recent Mac, and every native editor on this page needs it.
Overleaf if co-authors need to edit the same document live, or you are on a
machine you cannot install 5 GB on. Many people use both.

### Which LaTeX compiler should I use on a Mac?

pdfLaTeX, unless something forces a change. It is the default in every
editor here and what journal templates assume. Use XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX when
you need system fonts or full Unicode. All three ship with MacTeX.

## Tools that work alongside any of these

Whichever editor you pick, these free in-browser utilities pair well:

- LaTeX to PDF: compile when you're on a machine without a TeX install.

- LaTeX to Word: convert your manuscript for journals that require .docx.

- LaTeX Diff: generate a tracked-changes PDF between two versions.

- BibTeX Validator: catch citation errors before compile.

Once the writing is done and submission is next, Paper Review red-teams the manuscript before a referee does: four reviewer personas argue over it, citations are checked against the live record, and figures are scanned for integrity problems. That one is paid, from $9 per review.

For more on the academic LaTeX workflow generally, see the LaTeX hub and the BibTeX and citations hub.
